title: ASCII, Unicode, UTF-8, and why emojis break things
story:
The American Standards Association published ASCII as X3.4-1963: a 7-bit code with 128 positions, covering the Latin letters, digits, punctuation and teletype control codes. One character, one byte, with a bit to spare. Every language and file format built in that era encoded the assumption, and the assumption held as long as the text was English.

It stopped holding as computing spread, and what followed was a proliferation of incompatible eight-bit extensions — one per region, each claiming the upper 128 positions for a different alphabet. A document written under one and read under another does not fail; it renders as the wrong letters, which is a worse outcome than an error because nothing reports it.

Then the fix, and the flaw in the fix, which is the part of this story worth actually knowing.

The Unicode project began in 1987 when Joe Becker, an engineer at Xerox, drafted a proposal for a universal 16-bit character set, and his report Unicode 88 was issued on 29 August 1988. It described the need for a reliable world text encoding — roughly a wide-body ASCII stretched to 16 bits to encompass the characters of the world's living languages — and argued that 16 bits per character were more than sufficient, that 65,536 code points would be enough for every character needed for modern communication. The work grew out of eight years of experience with Xerox's internal Character Code Standard.

The Unicode Consortium itself was formed on 3 January 1991 in California by Becker, Collins and Davis, with founding members including Apple, IBM, Microsoft, Xerox and Sun Microsystems. The first volume of The Unicode Standard was published in October 1991, and a second volume adding Han ideographs followed in June 1992.

And the 16-bit assumption did not survive. Unicode 2.0, in 1996, expanded the space to 1,114,112 code points across 17 planes — so the sufficiency argument at the centre of the original proposal was abandoned within five years of the standard's first volume.

That sentence is the actual cause of nearly every text bug you will meet. Languages and platforms designed between 1991 and 1996 took the 16-bit promise at face value and made a sixteen-bit unit their native character type. When the space grew beyond what sixteen bits can address, those systems could not change their fundamental unit without breaking everything already written, so they encoded the larger code points as pairs of sixteen-bit units instead. The pair is a workaround for a promise that was withdrawn, and it is permanent.

Which is why an emoji has a length of two in several major languages. It is one character to a reader and one code point to the standard, but it sits above the sixteen-bit range, so it occupies two of the units the language calls characters. Nothing is broken; a measurement is being reported in a unit that stopped meaning what its name implies in 1996.

UTF-8 is the other half of the story and it solved a different problem. Ken Thompson and Rob Pike designed it in September 1992, with Thompson working the encoding out on a placemat in a New Jersey diner. It is backward compatible with ASCII — every ASCII position keeps its single-byte representation — and encodes the rest of the space in sequences of two to four bytes. That backward compatibility is why it won: existing English text and existing byte-oriented tools kept working unchanged.

But variable width has its own consequence, and it is the one that produces corruption rather than confusion. A byte offset is no longer a character offset. Truncate a string to fit a byte limit and the cut can land in the middle of a multi-byte sequence, producing bytes that are not valid text at all — which is how a field limit intended to protect a column ends up storing something no decoder will accept.

So the honest summary has three layers, not one, and none of them is in fixed correspondence with the others. There is the character a reader perceives; the code point the standard assigns; and the bytes or code units that encode it. One reader-visible character can be several code points, and one code point can be several bytes or several sixteen-bit units. Every question about text has to specify which layer it is asking about, and most text bugs are a question answered in the wrong layer.

problem.name: Three layers of text
problem.shape: Something needs to know how long a string is, or where to cut it.
tell: a length check passes and the stored value is corrupt
a field limit is expressed in characters and enforced in bytes
text renders as the wrong letters rather than failing
a string looks one character long and reports a length of two or more
problem.move: Decide which layer the question is about before answering it: the characters a reader perceives, the code points the standard assigns, or the bytes and code units that encode them. Enforce limits in the unit the storage actually uses, and cut only at boundaries the encoding defines.
problem.invariant: Character, code point and encoded unit are three different things in no fixed correspondence. A count in one of them licenses no conclusion about the others.
problem.breaks: Even code points are not the reader's unit. A perceived character can be several code points — a base letter with combining marks, or an emoji assembled from a sequence with joiners — so counting code points is merely a better wrong answer than counting bytes, and the only correct unit for 'what a reader would call one character' is the grapheme cluster.

cost.time: indexing into variable-width text is a scan rather than an offset calculation, so operations that look constant-time are linear
cost.space: non-Latin text takes more bytes than its character count suggests, which makes byte-sized storage limits a language-dependent restriction on content
cost.beats: fixed-width encodings, which make indexing trivial and waste space and broke compatibility so thoroughly they were never widely adopted for interchange, and single-byte code pages, which are compact and cannot represent two alphabets at once

worked.problem: Why does a single emoji report a length of two in several major languages, and what bug does that cause against a database column limit?
worked.reasoning:
Because those languages count sixteen-bit code units rather than characters, and the emoji sits above the range a single sixteen-bit unit can address — so it occupies two of them. The deeper reason is historical and worth giving, because it explains why this cannot simply be fixed.

The Unicode project began in 1987 with Joe Becker's proposal for a universal 16-bit character set, and his report Unicode 88 of 29 August 1988 argued that 16 bits per character were more than sufficient — that 65,536 code points would be enough for every character needed for modern communication. The Consortium was formed on 3 January 1991 and the first volume of the standard published that October, so platforms designed in those years reasonably took the promise at face value and made a sixteen-bit unit their native character type.

Then the promise was withdrawn. Unicode 2.0, in 1996, expanded the space to 1,114,112 code points across 17 planes. The systems already built on sixteen bits could not change their fundamental unit without invalidating everything written against them, so they represented the larger code points as pairs of sixteen-bit units instead. That pair is scar tissue from a retracted assumption, and it is permanent — which is why the emoji is one character to a reader, one code point to the standard, and two units to the language.

Now the bug, which has a shape worth recognising because it is not a crash. Suppose a limit is enforced by counting the language's length and storage counts something else — bytes, in the case of UTF-8. An emoji is four bytes and reports a length of two, so a string that passes a length check can exceed the byte capacity of the column. The insert is rejected, or worse, the value is silently truncated at the byte boundary. And a byte-boundary cut can land in the middle of a multi-byte sequence, which produces bytes that are not valid text at all. The field limit intended to protect the column stores something no decoder will accept.

The general form is that a count was taken in one unit and a constraint applied in another. The fix is not a clever length function; it is to enforce the limit in the unit the storage uses, and to cut only at boundaries the encoding defines.

I would add the correction that keeps this from becoming a false sense of safety, because 'count code points instead' is the usual next answer and it is also wrong. A perceived character can be several code points — a base letter with combining marks, or an emoji assembled from a sequence joined together. So counting code points is a better wrong answer than counting bytes. The only unit corresponding to what a reader would call one character is the grapheme cluster, and it is the one no language makes convenient.

The reason all of this is unavoidable rather than merely annoying is worth stating in one line: there are three layers — the perceived character, the code point, and the encoded unit — and no two of them are in fixed correspondence. Every question about text has to name its layer, and most text bugs are a question answered in the wrong one.

problem.practice: Take a text field in your own system and find out which unit its limit is expressed in and which unit the storage enforces. Then put an emoji and a letter with a combining accent through it and see whether the two agree.

beats.broke: A character was assumed to be a byte, then assumed to be sixteen bits — and each assumption was built into languages and file formats before it turned out to be false.
beats.fix: Separate the three layers that got conflated: the character a reader perceives, the code point the standard assigns, and the bytes or code units that encode it.
beats.cost: The failed sixteen-bit assumption is permanent in the systems built on it, which is why length has one answer in bytes, another in code units, another in code points and another in what a reader would call characters.

interview.q: Why does a single emoji report a length of two in several major languages, and what bug does that cause against a database column limit?
interview.trap: Assuming the length is counting visible characters. It is counting sixteen-bit code units — and the usual correction, counting code points instead, is also wrong, because a perceived character can be several code points.
interview.answer:
Because those languages count sixteen-bit code units, and the emoji sits above the range one such unit can address, so it takes two. The historical reason is worth giving, because it explains why it cannot simply be fixed.

Joe Becker's Unicode 88 report of 29 August 1988 proposed a universal sixteen-bit set and argued that sixteen bits per character were more than sufficient — that 65,536 code points would be enough for every character needed for modern communication. Underneath all of it: three layers — perceived character, code point, encoded unit — and no two in fixed correspondence. Most text bugs are a question answered in the wrong layer.
